Survivor & Thriver Fund, LP 
 
2025 Annual Partnership Letter 
 
Dear Partner, 
Two thousand and twenty-five was a good, yet choppy year for our fund. In 4Q the 
fund was down -7.5% bringing the full year return to +21.8% net to investors. This compares to the 
S&P 500 which gained 3.1% in 4Q and 17.7% for the full year assuming dividends had been 
immediately reinvested back into the index. 
In last year's annual letter I talked about the acceleration of technological change that I saw 
happening in sectors and companies I follow. What a difference a year makes. 
Conversations about using LLMs for everything from tax advice to holiday planning now feel 
commonplace. New agents are emerging that are increasingly capable across a wide range of tasks, 
from coding to managing personal stuff. Teenagers discuss viral songs that were not created by a 
human, or the new short video series on TikTok produced by a single creator. People remark on how 
nice high-speed Starlink internet is on a flight, and how cool it was to experience a driverless taxi for 
the first time. 
I am fully aligned with the view that many tasks currently performed by humans will increasingly be 
handled by hardware controlled by a software “brain” that learns and improves on its own. As this 
happens, use cases for products can expand beyond narrow, sector-specific verticals like “ride-
sharing” or “warehouse” into broader categories su

While we do not own any enterprise software stocks but the correction has also spread wider, such 
as to our high free-cash-flow generative consumer tech names. I am actively sifting through the 
dislocation for new ideas. We are not looking for collapsed stocks hoping for a bounce. Instead, we 
want to own companies with similar characteristics to what we own today, and with business 
models positioned to get stronger as AI tools improve. 
As token prices continue to decline and new chip designs enable lightning-fast, low-power inference, 
monetization models [of everything] are likely to shift to consumption-based. For the right 
businesses this will unlock TAM that was previously out of reach. 
For example, smaller consumer platforms such as Spotify will be able to build Facebook-like 
recommendation engines, powered by new inference-as-a-service offerings that were cost 
prohibitive even a year ago. More effective recommendation engines should enable more effective 
performance-based advertising and support a higher take rate on product-driven transactions. In 
many categories there will be meaningful winners that the market is currently overlooking.

My point is that with so much rapid change, identifying tomorrow's winners is not as easy as running 
a screen on historical earnings. When the past is less of a reference for the future, identifying 
durability is more qualitative, subjective and difficult because it often goes against consensus. 
Since the future is so uncertain we look for businesses with moats that are protecting market 
position in a market that is growing. We want leadership that can evolve quickly when others can't. 
We also want secular tailwinds and structural advantages that will be more important in tomorrow's 
economy. In our case this could mean owning a large global platform where customer behavioral 
data is used to enhance products, deepen customer relationships and drive pricing power. 
Lastly, we need to feel good about the price we pay relative to the business's opportunity set over a 
reasonable time horizon. Every stock in our portfolio was purchased at a time when the market was 
distracted by economic uncertainty or a business or sector transition that overshadowed underlying 
earnings power.

Implications to upside potential 
Pure is positioned at the center of a secular shift as flash storage replaces hard drives across 
enterprise, hyperscale, and AI-adjacent workloads. 
Estimates for market size range from $65 billion by 2031 (Mordor Intelligence) to $132 billion by 
2035 (Future Market Insights), up from roughly $20 billion today. Pure's own TAM framework 
estimates the all-flash array market will grow >20% annually for the next ~5 years (company 
presentations). 
As AI inference and data-intensive applications scale, storage could move from a cyclical purchase to 
a capacity layer, structurally enlarging the lifetime spend per customer. 
Starting from roughly $630 million of FY26 non-GAAP operating income, Pure has a credible path to 
$2+ billion of operating earnings over the next five years. This is supported by market expansion, 
share gains in flash, and operating leverage as recurring revenue becomes the majority of revenue. 
In our bull case, Pure's operating margins could settle out in the mid 30% range with returns on 
capital between 30% and 40%, and a debt-free balance sheet. 
In this scenario the valuation would support a 30x to 40x multiple on $2 billion of GAAP operating 
earnings implying a $60 to $80 billion enterprise value versus $20 billion today. Although Pure might 
screen expensive, we think the fundamental downside case is limited because of Pure's market 
position and

Although 4Q'25 earnings are not out yet, the company estimates it will end 2025 with 745 million 
users, up by 100 million over 2024. 
Since we've owned the stock, Spotify has added over 530 million users. Operating income has gone 
from near-breakeven, to what we think will be north of US$3.5 billion in 2026. 
Gross margin, operating income and free cash flow continue to grow faster than revenue with gains 
operating leverage across the platform. 
By our estimates, 2025 operating earnings grew by ~56% and free cash flow was up about 26%. This 
was driven by subscriber growth, price increases for the premium tier and increased use of the two-
sided marketplace. 
The hand that feeds the music industry 
 
In 2025 Spotify paid out about $11 billion to the recorded music industry. With the global recorded 
music market estimated to have generated roughly $30 billion, Spotify represented around 36% of 
total industry revenue and about 50% of all streaming revenue generated for the music industry.6 
 
Spotify is the music industry's consumer engagement layer and outsourced technology partner. In 
return, Spotify collects and owns personal behavioral data that it uses to analyze patterns across 
users as shared preferences for mood, styles and listening contexts. This understanding allows the 
system to predict what users might like and build personalized music, podcast and audiobook
